title: THE MOST DANGEROUS WORDS IN CHRISTIANITY MIGHT BE: “I’M SAVED, SO I’M FINE.”
paragraphs: THE MOST DANGEROUS WORDS IN CHRISTIANITY MIGHT BE: “I’M SAVED, SO I’M FINE.”

The terrifying possibility of knowing the language of salvation while slowly losing your hunger for the Savior—and why Jesus still calls the comfortable, the compromised, and the spiritually exhausted back to Himself.
There is something more frightening than a sinner who knows he is lost.
It is a religious person who is absolutely convinced he has nothing left to repent of.
Read that again.
Because somewhere tonight, a man will close his Bible without allowing a single word to confront him.
A woman will whisper a hurried prayer while carrying bitterness she has no intention of surrendering.
A husband will sing about the love of Christ on Sunday and return home to wound his family with the same tongue that praised God.
“I’m saved, so I’m fine.”
And perhaps the most unsettling part is that none of them necessarily look like people who have abandoned Christianity.
They still believe in God.
They still know the songs.
They still share Bible verses.
They may even defend sound doctrine with extraordinary confidence.

But somewhere between receiving the message of grace and becoming comfortable with its vocabulary, they have stopped asking whether their lives are actually being transformed by the Savior they profess.
Before you assume this article is about someone else, there is a question worth carrying all the way to the end.
What if the greatest danger to your spiritual life is not that you have stopped believing in Jesus, but that you have become comfortable claiming His name while resisting His voice?
That question is not an accusation that every struggling Christian is unsaved.
It is an invitation to something far more serious than religious insecurity.
It is an invitation to honest examination before the God who already knows us completely.
Because Jesus never called us to build our confidence on how convincingly we can say, “I am saved.”
He calls us to trust Him.
And genuine trust in Christ is not meant to leave us indifferent to the One we claim has rescued us.
There is a moment in the Gospel of Matthew that should make every professing Christian stop.
Jesus is speaking about the final judgment.
He describes people who address Him with extraordinary religious familiarity.
They do not call Him a stranger.
They call Him Lord.
Twice.
“Lord, Lord.”
They even point to impressive religious works performed in His name.
And yet Jesus says:
“I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity.” — Matthew 7:23, KJV
Those words are devastating.
Not because Jesus is teaching that genuinely saved people can suddenly lose their salvation through an ordinary failure.

Christians have historically differed on questions about perseverance and apostasy, but the warning in this passage is unmistakable: an outward profession of faith, even accompanied by remarkable religious activity, is not itself proof of belonging to Christ.
Notice what Jesus does not say.
He does not say, “I knew you once, but then I forgot you.”
He says, “I never knew you.”
The issue is not that they lacked religious vocabulary.
They had plenty.
The issue is that their claims about Him did not correspond to a genuine relationship of faith expressed in obedience.
And that should humble every one of us.
Because it is possible to be recognized in a church and still be unknown to the people sitting beside you.
It is possible to have an impressive ministry reputation while concealing a life that desperately needs repentance.
It is possible to spend years talking about Jesus without honestly listening to what Jesus says.
The Greek text of Matthew 7:23 contains the words:
οὐδέποτε ἔγνων ὑμᾶς
Oudépote égnōn hymâs.
“I never knew you.”
The word οὐδέποτε (oudepote) means “never” or “not at any time.”
And ἔγνων (egnōn) comes from the verb ginōskō, meaning “to know.”
In this context, Jesus is speaking of recognition within a genuine relationship, not a lack of information. The omniscient Son of God is not saying He was unaware these people existed.
He is declaring that their religious claims did not make them His.

Imagine standing before the One whose name you used in prayers, songs, arguments, and public declarations, only to discover that your confidence had rested on religious performance rather than on Christ Himself.
That is not a scene Jesus gave us so we could speculate about who else might be condemned.
He gave the warning so that we would listen.
So that we would stop mistaking familiarity with Christianity for living faith in Christ.
So that we would not confuse a public testimony with the inward reality to which that testimony should point.
And perhaps that is where this becomes painfully personal.
Because most spiritual drifting does not begin with someone waking up and declaring, “I no longer want Jesus.”
Sometimes it begins with a small compromise.
A little dishonesty.
A private habit defended as harmless.
A grudge protected for years.
A secret conversation you would never want your spouse to read.
A pattern of cruelty excused because you were tired, hurt, or misunderstood.
At first, your conscience protests.
You feel the weight of what you have done.
You pray.
You confess.
You struggle.
But after repeating the same compromise, something changes.
Not necessarily your church attendance.
Not necessarily your theology.
Something quieter.
Your willingness to be corrected.
You begin explaining away what you once confessed.
You start calling conviction “judgment.”
You mistake accountability for rejection.
And whenever the truth comes close enough to threaten your comfort, you reach for a familiar defense.
“God knows my heart.”
Yes.
He does.
And that is precisely why the statement should lead us toward humility rather than self-justification.
He knows the wounds nobody sees.
He knows the temptations you are fighting.
He knows when you are genuinely trying to obey and stumbling along the way.
But He also knows when repentance has been replaced by excuses.
He knows the difference between a believer who hates his sin and a person who has made peace with it.
And the answer to that knowledge is not despair.
It is to come into the light.
The apostle John wrote:
“If we say that we have fellowship with him, and walk in darkness, we lie, and do not the truth.” — 1 John 1:6, KJV
But John does not leave us trembling in that warning.
Just three verses later, he writes:
Do you see the beauty?
The same passage that refuses to flatter our darkness opens the door to forgiveness.
Christianity is not the announcement that people who belong to Jesus never sin.
John explicitly rejects that idea in 1 John 1:8.
Christianity is the announcement that sinners have an Advocate, Jesus Christ the righteous, and that His sacrifice is sufficient for those who come to Him in faith.
The danger is not that you still need grace.
We all do.
The danger is deciding that grace makes repentance unnecessary.
Because grace is not permission to remain enslaved.
Grace is God's undeserved favor that brings us to Christ and begins teaching us to live differently.
Paul makes this unmistakable in Titus 2:11–12.
He writes that the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation, and that this grace teaches us to deny ungodliness and worldly desires and live godly lives.
In the Greek, the word translated “teaching” is παιδεύουσα (paideuousa).
It carries the sense of training, educating, or disciplining.
That is a remarkable picture.
Grace does not merely announce pardon.
Grace trains.
Grace corrects.
Grace forms a new way of life.
Not because our obedience purchases salvation, but because the grace that saves us also begins transforming us.
And this is where a dangerous misunderstanding must be confronted.
Some people hear a message about repentance and immediately fear that their salvation depends on achieving moral perfection.
Others hear a message about salvation by grace and conclude that their choices no longer matter.
Both misunderstand the Gospel.
Ephesians 2:8–9 teaches that we are saved by grace through faith, not by works.
But verse 10 continues by saying that we are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
The order matters.
We are not saved because we have transformed ourselves.
We are saved by God's grace, through faith in Christ, and that salvation is intended to bear fruit in our lives.
Good works are not the price of redemption.
They are a fitting response to redemption.
And no Christian should turn that truth into a weapon against someone who is sincerely struggling.
There is a difference between fighting sin and defending it.
A difference between falling and deciding never to rise.
A difference between a wounded believer crying out for help and a hardened heart refusing to hear God's Word.
Consider Peter.
He made bold promises about his loyalty to Jesus.
He was certain of himself.
Certain he would stand.
Certain he would never deny his Lord.
Then came the courtyard.
The questions.
The fear.
And the terrible sound of his own voice denying that he knew Jesus.
Three times.
Then the rooster crowed.
Luke 22:61 tells us that the Lord turned and looked at Peter.
Imagine that moment.
The man who had promised to die for Jesus had just denied knowing Him.
And now he was looking into the face of the One he had betrayed.
Peter went outside and wept bitterly.
He could not hide behind his previous declarations.
He could not appeal to his years of ministry experience.
He could not pretend the denial had not happened.
But Peter's failure was not the final word of his story.
After His resurrection, Jesus met him again.
In John 21, Jesus asked Peter about his love and entrusted him with the care of His sheep.
There is a detail here worth handling carefully.

John's Greek account uses both ἀγαπάω (agapaō) and φιλέω (phileō), words associated with love and affection. Some interpretations build a sharp distinction between them, but John's Gospel often uses these terms interchangeably. The central emphasis of the passage is not a secret code hidden in the vocabulary.
It is the risen Christ restoring a fallen disciple and calling him back to faithful service.
Peter had denied Jesus three times.
And now, in a deeply personal encounter, Jesus questioned Peter's love three times.
The restoration was not cheap.
It did not pretend the betrayal was insignificant.
But neither did Jesus discard Peter as though his failure were beyond redemption.
That is the Gospel's astonishing beauty: Jesus does not excuse our sin, and He does not refuse the repentant sinner who comes to Him.
Perhaps you need to hear that.
Perhaps you have spent months living with the shame of something you did.
Perhaps you still remember the words you spoke when anger overtook you.
Perhaps your family knows a version of you that your church has never seen.
Perhaps your prayer life has become a collection of apologies that you are afraid to believe God still hears.
Or perhaps your situation is the opposite.
You have not felt convicted in a long time.
You are comfortable.
Religious.
Respected.
And increasingly unmoved by the things of God.
The Gospel speaks to both conditions.
To the broken, Jesus offers mercy.
To the complacent, Jesus calls for repentance.
To the self-righteous, Jesus exposes false confidence.
To the exhausted believer, Jesus offers rest.
And to every one of us, He says something far better than “Pretend you are fine.”
He says:
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” — Matthew 11:28, KJV
Not “Come when you have made yourself worthy.”
Not “Come when your spiritual record looks impressive.”
Come to Me.
That invitation is not a promise that discipleship will never be difficult.
It is a promise that our deepest hope is found in a Person, not in our ability to maintain an appearance.
And now we need to talk about one of the most uncomfortable passages in the New Testament.
Revelation 3.
The church in Laodicea.
A community that believed it was rich, prosperous, and in need of nothing.
But Jesus saw something very different.
He described their condition as lukewarm.
The passage includes a severe warning, followed by a profoundly tender invitation.
Jesus says:
“As many as I love, I rebuke and chasten: be zealous therefore, and repent.” — Revelation 3:19, KJV
Do not miss the first part.
“As many as I love.”
His rebuke was not presented as evidence that He had ceased to care.
It was a call to wake up.
The Greek word translated “repent” is μετανόησον (metanoēson), an imperative form of metanoeō.
It means to repent—to turn from a wrong course with a changed understanding and disposition.
Biblical repentance is more than a passing feeling of regret.
It involves turning toward God, and it bears fruit in the way we live.
Then comes Revelation 3:20.
“Behold, I stand at the door, and knock.”
That verse is often quoted in evangelistic invitations. But in its immediate context, Jesus is addressing a church.
A church that had become self-satisfied.
A church that needed to hear His voice again.
And the astonishing thing is that Christ calls them to respond.
Not to protect their reputation.
Not to produce a more impressive religious performance.
But to repent and receive renewed fellowship with Him.
How many of us have become experts at looking spiritually successful while quietly neglecting communion with Jesus?
How many of us know how to encourage everyone else but cannot remember the last time we were genuinely honest with God?
How many of us are willing to defend the Bible in an argument but unwilling to obey it when it confronts our pride?
That question is not only for pastors.
Not only for ministry leaders.
Not only for people who have fallen publicly.
It is for the person writing these words.
And it is for the person reading them.
For all of us.
Because no one becomes spiritually mature by declaring themselves beyond correction.
Paul himself wrote:
“Wherefore let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall.” — 1 Corinthians 10:12, KJV
This was not an invitation to live in perpetual terror.
It was a warning against presumption.
Against the dangerous confidence that says, “That could never happen to me.”
You may love Jesus deeply and still need correction.
You may have walked with Him for decades and still need to surrender an attitude you have protected.
You may have a genuine testimony of salvation and still need to confess the way you have treated someone.
And you may be at the very beginning of faith, uncertain about many things, yet sincerely reaching toward Christ.
The question is not whether your Christian life looks as polished as someone else's.
The question is where your confidence rests and whether you are willing to hear the Shepherd's voice.
Jesus says in John 10:27:
“My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.”
Notice the beautiful balance.
“I know them.”
That is security rooted in the Shepherd.
“They follow me.”
That is the direction of a living relationship.
Not flawless performance.
Not sinless perfection.
But belonging to Christ and responding to Him.
And in the very next verses, Jesus speaks of giving His sheep eternal life and keeping them securely in His hand.
That matters.
Because an article warning against spiritual complacency must never leave a sincere believer thinking that one failure has placed them beyond the mercy of God.
Your salvation is not sustained by your ability to be impressive.
Christ is a sufficient Savior.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.”
The assurance of salvation is not arrogance when it is grounded in God's promises and genuine faith in His Son.
The dangerous statement is not simply “I am saved.”
Scripture gives believers reasons for real assurance.
The danger comes when “I am saved” becomes a shield against repentance, a substitute for obedience, or an excuse to ignore the Word of God.
There is a world of difference between saying, “Jesus has saved me, and I trust Him,” and saying, “Jesus has saved me, so I no longer need to listen to Him.”
One is the language of faith.
The other can become the language of presumption.
And perhaps the most important question is no longer whether you can remember the day you first professed faith.
Perhaps it is whether the Christ you profess is the Christ you are willing to follow today.
Not perfectly.
But sincerely.
Not without struggle.
But without making peace with darkness.
Not because you are trying to earn His love.
But because His love has reached you.
There is a reason the writer of Hebrews urges believers to encourage one another daily so that none may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin (Hebrews 3:13).
Sin deceives.
It rarely introduces itself as destruction.
It presents itself as relief.
As entitlement.
As something you deserve after everything you have endured.
It tells you that bitterness is protection.
That revenge is justice.
That secrecy is harmless.
That compromise is freedom.
And sometimes, most dangerously, it borrows the language of grace.
“God will forgive me anyway.”
Yes, God's mercy is astonishing.
But Romans 6:1–2 directly rejects the idea that grace should encourage us to continue in sin.
Paul asks whether we should continue in sin so that grace may abound.
His answer is emphatic:
“God forbid.”
The Greek expression is μὴ γένοιτο (mē genoito).
It is a forceful rejection, often understood as “By no means!” or “May it never be!”
Paul is not uncertain.
Grace is not an argument for remaining under sin's dominion.
It is the foundation of a new life in Christ.
And now, imagine a different kind of evening.
The house is quiet.
Your phone is face down.
Nobody is watching.
There is no church audience to impress.
No comment section to defend yourself in.
No religious reputation to maintain.
Just you.
Your memories.
Your compromises.
Your disappointments.
The prayers you stopped praying.
The Scripture you have been avoiding.
And the God who already knows every part of the story.
What would happen if you stopped trying to convince Him you were fine?
What if you said:
“Lord Jesus, I have been calling myself strong when I am actually afraid.”
“I have been calling my bitterness wisdom.”
“I have been calling my compromise a weakness I do not need to confront.”
“I have been hiding behind what I know about You while neglecting my relationship with You.”
“Forgive me.”
“Teach me to walk in Your truth.”
“Change what I cannot change by my own strength.”
There is no magic formula in those words.
Salvation does not come through reciting a particular script.
But there is something profoundly biblical about bringing the truth into God's presence and seeking His mercy through Christ.
Psalm 51 gives us the language of a repentant heart.
After his grievous sin, David prayed:
“Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.” — Psalm 51:10, KJV
In Hebrew, the opening words are:
לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים
Lev tahor bera-li Elohim.
“Create for me a clean heart, O God.”
The verb בְּרָא (bera) comes from the Hebrew root bara, “to create.”
David is asking God to do something that goes deeper than outward religious repair.
He is asking for inward renewal.
He does not merely ask to look clean.
He asks for a clean heart.
And perhaps that is the prayer we have been avoiding.
Because it is easier to ask God to change our circumstances than to ask Him to confront what is wrong within us.
Easier to pray for success than for humility.
Easier to pray for protection than to admit where we have hurt others.
Easier to ask for blessings than to surrender the habits that keep us spiritually distracted.
Yet the God who exposes our sin is also the God who welcomes repentant sinners.
And at the center of that hope stands a cross.
Not our religious résumé.
Not our church attendance.
Not our ministry accomplishments.
Not the number of Bible verses we can quote.
A cross.
Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, gave Himself for sinners.
He bore our sins, died, and rose again.
The resurrection declares that our hope is not in a dead teacher whose advice might improve our lives.
Our hope is in the living Lord who has conquered death.
The cross tells us that sin is too serious to dismiss.
The resurrection tells us that sin and death do not have the final word for those who belong to Him.
This is why the Gospel is not merely self-improvement.
It is redemption.
It is reconciliation with God.
It is the gift of new life through Jesus Christ.
And it is why the theme we carry at Gospel Warrior is more than a memorable phrase.
Not because Jesus pretends the scandal never happened.
Not because consequences always disappear.
Not because repentance automatically repairs every relationship we have damaged.
Sometimes restoration requires difficult apologies.
Sometimes it requires restitution.
Sometimes it requires patient rebuilding of trust.
Sometimes it requires accepting consequences without demanding that others immediately forgive, reconcile, or restore access.
But the Gospel declares that the worst chapter of a repentant sinner's life does not have to become the final definition of that life.
Think of the woman caught in adultery in John 8.
Jesus did not join the crowd in condemning her.
And He did not call her sin harmless.
His words held mercy and moral seriousness together.
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.”
Mercy did not mean indifference.
Grace did not mean permission.
Jesus offered a future that was not meant to be a repetition of the past.
That is the kind of Savior we proclaim.
One who welcomes sinners.
One who confronts hypocrisy.
One who restores the fallen.
One who calls His people to holiness.
One who remains faithful even when our strength is small.
And one whose grace is powerful enough to make real change possible.
Perhaps you are reading this with tears in your eyes.
Perhaps you have been fighting the same temptation for years.
Perhaps you are ashamed that your spiritual life has grown cold.
Perhaps you have been hurt by Christians who spoke about grace but showed you very little of it.
Please hear this carefully.
You do not need to pretend that you are spiritually fine to come to Jesus.
And you do not need to believe that your struggles make you unworthy of seeking His help.
The weary are invited.
The burdened are invited.
The repentant are invited.
The spiritually complacent are called to wake up.
And the self-righteous are called to abandon their confidence in themselves.
All of us need the same Savior.
If this message has uncovered something you have been hiding, you do not have to publish the details of your struggle for strangers to read.
But perhaps you can take one small, sincere step toward the light today.

If Christ has been patiently transforming you through seasons of failure, repentance, and healing, share a word of testimony. Someone who feels beyond restoration may need to hear that Jesus has not abandoned His work in you.
And if this article brought someone to mind, consider sending it to them privately with compassion rather than accusation.
Not “This is about you.”
But “This challenged me, and I thought we could reflect on it together.”
You never know who is quietly reading.
The friend who has stopped praying.
The father who feels unworthy to return to God.
The young believer who thinks temptation has disqualified them.
The person who has confused church attendance with a relationship with Christ.
The unbeliever who has only encountered a version of Christianity that seems more interested in appearances than grace.
Not as a badge of spiritual seriousness.
For the day when you need to remember that conviction can be a mercy.
For the day when shame whispers that there is no way back.
Return to the Scriptures.
Return to the promises of Christ.
Return to the truth that the Savior who calls us to repentance is also mighty to save.
This is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to gather an audience that merely agrees with Christian statements.
Not to build a community that mistakes emotional reactions for spiritual maturity.
But to keep directing people to Scripture, to the real Jesus Christ, to the Gospel of grace, and to a life of growing discipleship.
Because one article may stir the heart.
But a disciple needs more than one stirring moment.
We need ongoing nourishment.
We need sound biblical teaching.
We need reminders when we forget.
We need encouragement when we are weary.
We need correction when we drift.
We need fellow believers who will help us remember that Christianity is not simply a label we carry but a life of faith in the risen Christ.
There is room here for the searching.
For the struggling.
For the believer who wants to grow.
For the person who is tired of shallow religious motivation and longs to understand the Bible more faithfully.
And for those who want to help this ministry continue reaching more people, there is an opportunity to go deeper.
It does not purchase salvation, forgiveness, spiritual protection, or a greater standing before Christ.
Those blessings cannot be bought.
But it can be a meaningful, voluntary expression of generosity and partnership in Gospel ministry.
If you have been looking for a way to support Gospel-centered work beyond simply reading and reacting, this is one practical opportunity.
Not from guilt.
Not from fear.
But because you believe the Gospel is worth sharing and want to help make that work possible.
Scripture reminds us in 2 Corinthians 9:7 that giving should not be reluctant or compelled, for God loves a cheerful giver.
If you are able and genuinely want to partner with this mission, we would be grateful to have you stand with us.
These are simply expressions of appreciation, not spiritual rewards or measures of faithfulness.
These resources are intended to help believers become more deeply rooted in Scripture, more discerning in their faith, and more devoted to Jesus Christ.
And that distinction matters.
Because Gospel Warrior is not here to place a price on access to Jesus.
We are here to point people to Him.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
Your willingness to share biblical truth matters.
Following Gospel Warrior can help you stay connected with daily Scripture, encouragement, biblical teaching, and opportunities to grow in discipleship.
Inviting someone to read, reflect, and open the Bible for themselves can become part of a much larger story of Gospel witness.
The mission is not to make people dependent on Gospel Warrior.
It is to help people grow in their knowledge of and dependence on Jesus Christ.
And before you leave, there is one final scene I want you to imagine.
Not a church building.
Not a stage.
Not a crowded revival meeting.
Just an ordinary room.
A person sitting alone.
A Bible nearby.
A heart that has grown tired of pretending.
Perhaps the person has been a Christian for forty years.
Perhaps for four months.
Perhaps they are not even certain they truly believe.
But for the first time in a long time, they stop defending themselves.
They stop comparing themselves with worse sinners.
They stop pointing to the good things they have done.
They stop repeating, “I'm saved, so I'm fine,” as though those words could settle every question about their spiritual condition.
And instead they turn toward Christ.
“Jesus, I need You.”
Not just yesterday.
Not just on the day I first believed.
Today.
“I need Your mercy.”
“I need Your truth.”
“I need Your forgiveness.”
“I need You to teach me how to follow You.”
And there, in that quiet honesty, something important happens.
Not necessarily an overwhelming emotion.
Not necessarily a dramatic experience.
But a heart is brought again to the truth.
The Christian life was never meant to be sustained by pretending we have no need.
It is sustained by the grace of God, through the living Christ, as the Holy Spirit works in us and draws us into obedience.
The apostle Paul writes in Philippians 1:6 that He who began a good work in believers will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ.
That promise is not an excuse for spiritual laziness.
It is hope for imperfect believers who trust the faithfulness of God.
And 2 Corinthians 13:5 calls us to examine ourselves to see whether we are in the faith.
So examine yourself.
But do not stop at yourself.
Look to Christ.
Confess what needs confessing.
Turn from what needs abandoning.
Seek help where help is needed.
Make right what you can.
Open the Word again.
Pray again.
Walk in the light.
And if you have never truly placed your faith in Jesus Christ, do not confuse a religious upbringing, a church membership, or an emotional memory with the saving work of the Lord.
Hear the Gospel.
Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures.
He was buried.
He rose again on the third day.
Repent and believe in Him.
Your hope is not in how confidently you can describe yourself as saved.
Your hope is in the Savior who is able to save.
And if you already belong to Him, you do not have to live every day in terror that your next mistake will exhaust His mercy.
Come to Him with confidence grounded in His grace, with humility before His Word, and with a willingness to follow wherever He leads.
Because the goal of Christianity is not to become someone who never admits needing Jesus.
It is to know Him, trust Him, love Him, and increasingly reflect His character.
Have I been resting in the finished work of Christ, or have I been using the language of salvation to avoid surrendering something He has been calling me to confront?
Do not rush past the answer.
Because someone may be one honest prayer away from turning back toward the Lord.
Someone may be reading these words while quietly wondering whether they have wandered too far.
Someone may need to hear that Jesus is not impressed by religious pretending, but He is merciful to sinners who come to Him.
And someone may finally understand that the Gospel is not the story of how good people proved they were worthy.
It is the story of how the holy Son of God came to save sinners.
That is why we keep writing.
That is why we keep sharing.
That is why we keep pointing beyond ourselves.
To Jesus.
Always to Jesus.
Because the most frightening place to be is not on your knees admitting how desperately you need a Savior—it is standing proudly in your religion, convinced you no longer need to listen to Him.
